text:
Mina: quick follow-up from the rate/quotas RFC — we need to lock down the enforcement boundary and a rollout plan for fairness + abuse prevention. want to align before monday.
Sam: two big decisions: 1) strong enforcement in the ingress (edge) vs 2) enforcement in runtime. ingress gives early fail and cheaper checks, runtime has more context (model, tokens). tradeoffs?
Andrew: agree. ingress is great for rough fairness and dodging abusive spikes. but for token quotas we need runtime counters (kv-cache, batching) to account for streaming tokens. hybrid sounds promising.
Julia: hybrid + a single source-of-truth quota service? ingress makes cheap checks using approximate counters, then runtime does final accounting. if mismatch, runtime can correct and emit correction metrics.
Mina: how do we implement "approximate counters" at edge? redis INCR is ok but will be hot for big customers. consider approximate sketch (space-saving) or sharded counters.
Sam: thought: use token-bucket at edge with per-key hashed shards. edge stores only a local bucket and periodically syncs deltas to quota service. keeps latency low and avoids global locks.
Andrew: downside: potential short-term over-commitment if a user hits multiple edges concurrently. we can cap burst window and make runtime enforce stricter post-check.
Julia: on abuse detection: we should run lightweight anomaly scoring at edge (rate-of-change, repeated failed auth, unusual model choices) — escalate suspicious traffic to a dedicated abuse queue that gets stricter limits.
Mina: flags: 1) consistency vs latency: strict global enforcement needs centralconsistency -> higher latency. 2) fairness policy language: simple weights vs hierarchical quotas for orgs/projects. prefer simple weights initially.
Sam: fairness algorithm options: weighted fair queuing (WFQ) vs proportional share via token buckets. WFQ gives smoother fairness but is heavier. token-buckets + priority queues likely easier to operate.
Andrew: would like an API surface: /quota/check (fast, returns allow/deny + ttl), /quota/charge (asyncable), /quota/rollback. runtime should call check then later call charge with final token count.
Julia: semantics for 429 vs 503: 429 for client exceeded quota, include Retry-After. 503 for transient capacity problems where fallback to cheaper model is suggested. include headers: X-Quota-Remaining, X-Quota-Unit
Mina: integrations: console UI needs per-key quota settings, and SLOs. Also alerts on sustained 90th percentile breaches.
Sam: storage choices: Redis cluster for low-latency counters, caveat: single-ops cost. We can use CockroachDB for durable quota history and Redis for hot counters.
Andrew: rollout plan: phase 0: edge checks + soft-deny (logs + metrics, header injection), phase 1: runtime enforcement for tokens, phase 2: strict denies + abuse queue + canary customers. propose 6-week phased rollout.
Julia: monitoring: counters, false-deny rate, correction deltas, latency added by checks, and abuse queue throughput. dashboards + periodic manual review of escalations.
Mina: one open question: should we proactively throttle heavy customers with an opt-out/reservation flow (reserved capacity)? affects product (Dedicated). thoughts?
Sam: yes, reserved capacity maps to Dedicated. add a flag in quota service that marks keys as "reserved" and bypass fairness pool, with billing tie-in.
Andrew: small sample config for runtime side:
```
quota_check: endpoint: /quota/check
max_burst_tokens: 300
weight: 1.0
reserved: false
```
Mina: action items: Sam to draft quota service API and sketch approximate edge algorithm, Andrew to prototype runtime charge/rollback, Julia to define metrics and dashboard. I'll consolidate into a short RFC update doc.
ops-bot: scheduled: quota-service-proto meeting set for 2026-03-24 10:00 UTC (reminder +30m)
Mina: thanks all — please add any missing objections now. if none, i'll post the RFC update tomorrow morning.
